extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and reformers interested in political economy and land reform (late 19th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A political‑economic critique arguing that private property in land is unjust, causes poverty and enslavement of labor, and proposing that land value (rent) belongs to the community rather than individual proprietors. The text diagnoses causes, gives historical examples, and rebuts common defenses (titles, priority, compensation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private property in land denies natural rights
rubrics_metrics.description: "The recognition of individual proprietorship of land is the denial of the natural rights of other individuals—it is a wrong which must show itself in the inequitable division of wealth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that because labour cannot produce without the use of land, denying equal right to use land denies labor its produce; this violation of the 'fundamental law of nature' results in unjust enrichment of a few and robbery of the many. Use this principle to judge the justice of any system of land tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land ownership appropriates the produce of labour via rent
rubrics_metrics.description: "If one man can command the land upon which others must labor, he can appropriate the produce of their labor as the price of his permission to labor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes rent as the mechanism by which landowners strip from laborers the wealth they justly earn; continuous increase of rent concentrates wealth in hands of those who do nothing to earn it. Use this criterion to evaluate whether a tenure system allows appropriation of labour's fruits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles resting on force or conquest lack moral validity
rubrics_metrics.description: "In California our land titles go back to the Supreme Government of Mexico, who took from the Spanish King, who took from the Pope... Everywhere, not to a right which obliges, but to a force which compels."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that historical grants, conquest, treaties, and royal grants are not equivalent to a just title; when title rests on force, the people (if they have power) may annul it. Use this standard to question legalistic defenses of existing land titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original title exists only to improvements, not to the land itself
rubrics_metrics.description: "To improvements such an original title can be shown; but it is a title only to the improvements, and not to the land itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that labour gives a rightful claim to the value added by improvements (clearing, draining), but not to exclusive proprietary title over the natural land. When improvements become blended with land, the greater (common right) swallows the less; this test distinguishes just claims from unjust monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value is the exact test distinguishing individual and common rights; rent measures community claim
rubrics_metrics.description: "A delicate and exact test is supplied by value... The value of land expresses in exact and tangible form the right of the community in land held by an individual; and rent expresses the exact amount which the individual should pay to the community to satisfy the equal rights of all other members of the community."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes using relative land value as the instrument to determine and secure equal rights: concede undisturbed use to prior occupiers but appropriate rent to the community. This is both a normative test and a practical policy prescription balancing incentives and equal rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of occupation does not justify complete and perpetual exclusive ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: "As for the deduction of a complete and exclusive individual right to land from priority of occupation... priority of appropriation one man could acquire and could transmit... a whole continent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects the argument that 'first comer' status grants unbounded exclusive rights; rights must be bounded by equal rights of others. Uses analogies (banquet, theatre, railroad car) to illustrate how priority cannot logically confer absolute exclusion; employ this when assessing claims based on first possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private land ownership inevitably tends toward enslavement of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ownership of land will always give the ownership of men, to a degree measured by the necessity (real or artificial) for the use of land... the enslavement of laborers the ultimate result of private property in land."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents thought experiments (one hundred men on an island) and historical examples (helotism, serfdom, latifundia) to show that ownership of land gives masters power over labourers, producing conditions equivalent to slavery as population pressure and monopolization increase. Use this criterion to judge social effects of tenure systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern wage conditions tend toward wages of slavery—only subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: "The wages of labor in the lower and wider strata of industry should everywhere tend to the wages of slavery—just enough to keep the laborer in working condition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains economic dynamic: as productive power increases, rent advances while wages fall; competition among laborers and monopoly of land convert labour into a commodity and laborers into machines. Use this to evaluate whether economic arrangements preserve substantive (not merely formal) freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolization of nature's gifts causes poverty and is unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: "Vice and misery, poverty and pauperism... only follow increase of population and industrial development because land is treated as private property—they are the direct and necessary results of the violation of the supreme law of justice..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributes social ills (pauperism, vice) to denial of equal natural rights via monopolization; critiques Malthusian defenses that blame nature rather than social institutions. Use this lens to diagnose causes of social poverty vs blaming natural scarcity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolishing private land need not (and should not) require compensating landowners
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is held... that if we abolish private property in land, justice requires that we should fully compensate those who now possess it..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects compensation rationales (government purchase at market price, resuming future increments) as morally and practically defective: compensating preserves landholder privileges and prevents remedying the underlying injustice; government purchase schemes are cumbersome, extend government functions, and invite corruption. Use this standard when evaluating reform proposals that seek to protect existing proprietor interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy prescription: confiscate rent for community while preserving undisturbed use (fixity of tenure)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thus, if we concede to priority of possession the undisturbed use of land, confiscating rent for the benefit of the community, we reconcile the fixity of tenure... with a full and complete recognition of the equal rights of all to the use of land."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a reconciliatory policy: allow individuals stability of tenure to encourage improvements and investment, but appropriate the land's rental value to the public. This provides a practical standard for designing land‑use and taxation reforms that respect both incentives and equal rights.
